The proposed acoustic cloak consists of alternating layers of water and Methyl Nonafluorobutyl Ether (MNE) embedded in an MNE substrate.
The mass densities of MNE and water are 1501 kg/m3 and 1482 kg/m3, respectively, and their sound velocities are 584 m/s and 998 m/s.
The multilayer cloak designs include 5-layer, 10-layer, and 20-layer structures with equal layer thicknesses.
The composite lattice cloak design has a constant 1.4 mm water layer thickness and gradually decreasing MNE layer thicknesses.
The acoustic cloaks are designed to operate at a frequency of 29 kHz, corresponding to a millimeter-scale structure with R1 = 15 mm, R2 = 35 mm, and r = 80 mm.
The homogeneous anisotropic cloak requires materials with anisotropic density and bulk modulus properties that are not readily available in nature.
Increasing the number of layers in the multilayer cloak from 5 to 10 to 20 improves the cloaking performance, approaching the ideal homogeneous anisotropic cloak.
The composite lattice cloak with gradually decreasing MNE layer thickness shows better cloaking performance than the multilayer cloak with equal layer thicknesses.
The proposed cloaks based on natural isotropic materials can operate over a wider frequency range compared to metamaterial-based cloaks.
The cloaking performance is evaluated using finite element method simulations of the total and scattered acoustic pressure fields.
The cloaking designs aim to minimize the scattering of the incident acoustic wave and conceal the object inside the cloak region.
The multilayer and composite lattice cloaks can hide objects of any shape within the cloak area.
Using natural materials like water and MNE simplifies the fabrication of the acoustic cloak compared to engineered metamaterials.
The cloaking designs are optimized to work in the kHz frequency range, avoiding high GHz frequencies where structural relaxation processes occur in the MNE polymer.
The proposed cloaking designs address the limitations of previous methods by providing a more practical and scalable approach to acoustic cloaking.
